name: Hana Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Hana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in new-homes sales for Bramley Partners, an agency that sells whole developments for builders. Right now I'm based in the show home at Orchard Rise, forty-two houses on the edge of town. I walk couples round the show home, explain the floor plans, take reservations, and then spend hours keeping buyers, solicitors and the builder's site manager in step.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the selling, and I enjoy being organised, so I've built my whole week around AI tools. I use one every day to answer enquiries, track every buyer's mortgage stage and draft updates. What wears me out is the builder missing completion dates and me being the one who tells the family their move is delayed again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good assistant and nothing more, which is how I already use it. I'd probably share my setup with the other negotiators. My dad would say he told me so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my small edge stays small. I'd still be faster than most, which helps my numbers. My pay is typical, I've got four months saved, and I rent a flat ten minutes from my parents, so life's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Bramley and push for the next big site, which is a hundred and twenty homes by the river. I'd keep saving towards buying a flat to live in and later rent out. And I'd keep refining my tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a bit bored, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New-homes sales depend on the builders. If interest rates stay high and builders slow down, there are fewer sites to sell. But Bramley has three builders on its books, so I'm not too worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would ask if I'm saving and going to the mosque on Fridays. Yes and yes. My dad would ask when I'll buy my own place, and I'd say two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and learn fast. I'd say it at work and online, because I believe it. I'd probably write about how new-homes sales can run on half the admin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this one is good for me. The other negotiators at Bramley spend half their time on admin I already automate. The firm would need fewer of us, and I'd be one of the ones they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd offer to roll out my setup across all of Bramley's show homes, for a bonus. I'd start planning my own small agency, just me and AI tools, selling for local builders who can't afford Bramley. I'd keep building my savings to six months before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A little guilty about colleagues, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a little guilty. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sarah, who's fifty and has been at the Orchard Rise show home for years. She hates computers. I'd try to help her, but I can't make her learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government should step in for people like Sarah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with handouts. With training on the job, so she can keep earning. Firms should do it, not the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, though even I'd be shaken. I'd probably post that people should look after their families first. I'd say it at the mosque too, where lots of the men run small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 a builder could sell a whole site with AI and one person in the show home. My planning and tracking, which I'm proud of, would be the first thing the AI does better. The show-home part lasts until robots, maybe 2031, but that's thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my small agency within six months, before everyone else thinks of it, and offer builders cheap all-in-one sales with AI and a human face. If it didn't work in a year, I'd move back in with my parents to save rent. I'd keep my savings for that first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but awake. I'd rather move fast than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back home at twenty-seven. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. In my family that's normal, and my parents would be happy. It's not failure if it saves money for something better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't starting a business risky when AI could replace it too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But being the person who sets up the AI is better than being the person the AI replaces. And builders still want someone to blame when the dates slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, but not much, so start now. I'd tell younger agents to save and learn the tools. I'd also say it to my brother, who's just starting at college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years means I can build the agency properly before 2031 and buy a flat while I'm earning. After 2031, I'd want to own property, not sell it for other people. The robots arriving later only helps the show-home side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Bramley for a year, learn the builder side, then go out on my own in 2028. I'd buy a small flat by 2029, live in it, and later rent it out. I'd try to have the agency employ one or two people by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but confident. I'd have a plan, and I like plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents think about you running a business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad ran a shop for twenty years, so he'd be proud. My mum would worry about me working too much and not getting married. She'd say that either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the business struggled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut costs fast, sell my tools to other small agencies, and keep the flat. Having something I own is the safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and hard work will be rewarded. I'd keep sharing tips online. I'd probably sound very relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years is enough to build a business, buy two flats and maybe start a family. By 2036 I'd want income from property, not from commission. That's a good life if I plan it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Bramley two or three years, then start my agency around 2029. I'd buy my first flat by 2028 and a second by 2032. I'd keep using every new AI tool as it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Ten years is enough for a plan to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe start a family. Would the ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might. I'd want to be married and settled before thirty-five. If the business and flats are set up, I'd feel safe having children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rents. If everyone loses commission jobs, who pays the rent on my flats? I'd have to keep them cheap and pick good areas.

I'd keep sharing **tips online** and sound relaxed.

By 2036 I want **income from property**, not commission.

S4.quote: By 2036 I'd want income from property, not from commission.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets her plan **business, flats and family**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build anything before the job went. What would help is cheap small-business loans for people starting out, and lower red tape for small agencies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether buyers would trust a one-person agency with AI. I think they would, if I'm honest and I turn up. People buy from people, even when the paperwork is done by a machine.

headlineQuote: People buy from people, even when the paperwork is done by a machine.

Traditional and **pro-business**, she prefers on-the-job training over handouts.
Wants to **start her own agency** and own flats, and stays calm with time.
